newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Algeria signs nuclear test ban treaty.
newsitem.headline: Algeria signs nuclear test ban treaty.

text.p: Algeria has signed the nuclear test ban treaty, one of 44 nations whose approval is necessary before the pact comes into force, the United Nations said on Wednesday.

The treaty now has signatures from 125 states since it was opened for signing on Sept. 24. But before it takes effect, 44 nations with nuclear power are required to sign and then ratify it through their national legislatures.
With Algeria's signature, only North Korea, India, Bangladesh and Pakistan of the 44 states have not signed and are not expected to do so in the near future.

India has vowed never to sign "this unequal treaty" until the declared atomic powers -- the United States, Russia, Britain, France and China -- devise a timetable for destroying their nuclear arsenals. And Pakistan has said it would not sign until India does.

The 40 with a nuclear potential who have signed, including the five nuclear powers, are Algeria, Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Egypt, Finland, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Iran, Israel, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Netherlands, Norway, Peru, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, South Korea, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, Ukraine, Vietnam and Zaire.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, followed by the other declared nuclear powers, signed the treaty to end all nuclear explosions on Sept. 24 . Clinton said signature of the pact was tantamount to a ban on testing "even before the treaty formally enters into force."
The treaty requires a conference in three to four years for members to decide how to speed up the ratification process should India and others still refuse to join the pact.
Fiji is the only state to have ratified the treaty and deposited papers to this effect with U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Monday.

The test ban treaty bans all explosions in the environment, whether in the atmosphere, space or underground, regardless of size. A 1963 treaty barred explosions in the atmosphere and another one in 1974 set a size limit on underground tests.
